h1: A horizontal whisky tasting by region
title: A Horizontal Whisky Tasting by Region | Craft Beer School
desc: How to run a horizontal whisky tasting across regions: picking comparable bottles, the order to taste and what regional style really tells you.
teaser: Same age, same cask style, different regions. A horizontal shows what place really adds.
standfirst: A horizontal tasting holds one thing steady, such as age, while the place changes. Lining up whiskies from different regions this way is the clearest test of whether regional style is real. Here is how to set one up.
sections:
In wine, a horizontal tasting means wines from the same vintage made by different producers. In whisky it usually means comparable whiskies from different distilleries or regions, holding something else constant: age, cask type or strength.

A vertical asks what changes within one distillery. A horizontal asks what changes between places. Our guide to a vertical tasting of one distillery covers the other approach.

The fairer the comparison, the more you learn. Try to match:

  • Age: for example, all around 10 to 12 years old.
  • Cask: all mainly ex-bourbon, or all sherry influenced.
  • Strength: similar ABV, or adjust with water.

A classic Scotch horizontal uses four regions: a Lowland, a Speyside, a Highland and an Islay single malt, all of similar age. That covers light and grassy, fruity, robust and smoky. Add Campbeltown if you can find one.

For a world horizontal, try a Scotch single malt, an Irish single pot still, a straight bourbon and an Indian single malt. The ages will not match, because climates differ so much, so note the age and judge maturity on the palate instead.
Taste light to heavy and keep pours small

Go from light to heavy. In a Scotch flight, that usually means Lowland, Speyside, Highland, then Islay. Smoke lasts on the palate and will distort anything tasted after it.

Pour 15 to 20 ml into identical tulip glasses. Nose each neat, then with a few drops of water. Taste in small sips. Drink water between glasses and wait a minute before the next.

Five glasses at 20 ml is 100 ml of whisky, more than most people should drink in an evening. Spit, or taste and leave the rest. Serve plain food and plenty of water. Cover glasses between sniffs in a warm room. Never drink and drive.

Reading regional differences confidently, rather than guessing from the label, comes from repeated structured comparisons. That is what trained tasting is built on.
What regional style really tells you

Scotch regions describe tendencies, not rules. Lowland malts are often light and grassy. Speyside malts are often fruity and elegant. Islay malts are often peated. But there are unpeated Islay malts and smoky Speyside malts. Our guides to Lowland whisky and island whiskies explain how much variety sits inside each label.

Much of what we call regional style comes from distillery choices that happen to cluster: peat levels, still shapes, cask policies. A horizontal often shows that the distillery's decisions matter more than the map. That is a useful lesson, not a disappointment.
Score each glass on the same scale

Use a simple sheet so the regions can be compared directly. For each glass, rate a few dimensions on a scale of 0 to 5:

  • Smoke
  • Fruit
  • Sweetness
  • Wood
  • Body

Then add three aroma words and a short note on the finish. Laid side by side, the scores show the regional differences as a pattern. It is the same idea as a spider chart in professional sensory panels. It works with pen and paper.

A horizontal is easier to read with one fixed reference point. Many tasters start every regional flight with the same whisky, a single malt they know well. They describe each new glass against it. Lighter or heavier? Fruitier or drier? More or less smoke?

Relative judgements are more reliable than absolute ones. Most people struggle to say exactly how smoky a whisky is on its own. Nearly everyone can say whether it is smokier than the glass next to it. Professional panels use reference samples for the same reason. Brewers do it when they taste a new batch beside the last good one.

Adding an Indian single malt to a Scotch flight is instructive. Indian heat speeds maturation, so a young Indian malt often shows more wood and richness than a Scotch of the same age. Matching by age makes the Indian malt seem oaky. Matching by perceived maturity is fairer.

It is also a good reminder that the word whisky covers very different products in India. Much of the market uses molasses spirit, which is a different category from malt whisky. Keep the flight to malt and grain whiskies if you want a fair comparison.
Run a three region flight first

Your first step: choose three Scotch single malts of similar age from the Lowlands, Speyside and Islay. Taste them light to heavy, score each on smoke, fruit and body and compare the scores. Three regions and three numbers will show you more than a map of all five.
faqs: What is a horizontal whisky tasting?
Tasting comparable whiskies from different distilleries or regions while keeping something constant, such as age or cask type.
What order should I taste regional whiskies in?
Light to heavy, usually Lowland, Speyside, Highland, then Islay, because smoke lingers on the palate.
Regions describe tendencies. Distillery choices such as peat level and cask policy often matter more.
